title: Weather: sun, rain, wind and clouds, and what to wear

summary.text: Sit in front of a fan and your arm feels cold. Yet a steel tumbler in the same wind gets no colder at all. Wind is moving air, and it carries your body's warmth away. Your child tests which clothes stop the fan's wind: a cotton dupatta, a thick woollen sweater, a thin raincoat and a newspaper. Then they learn the four kinds of weather, sunny, rainy, windy and cloudy, and what to wear for each.
summary.art: A child with one bare arm held out in front of a table fan, a steel tumbler standing in the same wind, and a pile of clothes on the floor: a sweater, a dupatta and a raincoat.

intro.hook: Switch on the fan and hold your bare arm in front of it. It feels cold. Now touch a steel tumbler that has stood in front of the fan for five minutes. Is the tumbler cold too?
intro.text: Guess first, and say why. Then touch it and find out. If the tumbler is not cold, why did your arm feel cold? In this unit we find out what wind does to a warm body. We test which clothes keep the wind out. And we look at sunny, rainy, windy and cloudy days, and how people all over India dress for each one.
intro.art: A child's hand touching a steel tumbler in front of a table fan, with a puzzled face, and a second tumbler on a shelf across the room.

outcomes: By the end I can name four kinds of weather: sunny, rainy, windy and cloudy.
By the end I can say that wind is moving air, and that it carries warmth away from my body.
By the end I can say which clothes stop the wind, and that a thick sweater does not.
By the end I can choose clothes for a sunny, a rainy, a windy and a cold day, and say why.
By the end I can say that clouds are made of tiny drops of water.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Weather is what the air and the sky are like outside, right now.
terms.example: Today the weather in Chennai is sunny and hot. In Shillong it is rainy and cool.
terms.art: Four small windows in a row: one with a bright sun, one with rain, one with a tree bending in the wind, one with grey clouds.

terms.meaning: Wind is air that is moving. We cannot see air, but we can see what wind moves.
terms.example: Wind flaps the clothes on the balcony line and blows dry leaves along the road.
terms.art: Clothes flapping on a balcony line, with leaves blowing along the street below.

terms.meaning: A cloud is made of millions of tiny drops of water, floating high in the air.
terms.example: Before the monsoon rain in Kochi, the sky fills with big grey clouds.
terms.art: A big grey cloud over coconut trees, with a zoom-in circle showing tiny round water drops.

terms.meaning: A layer is one piece of clothing worn on top of another.
terms.example: On a cold, windy hill, a thin rain jacket over a sweater is two layers.
terms.art: A child wearing a woollen sweater with a thin rain jacket on top, with a label pointing to each layer.

explanations.concept: Weather is what the air is doing
explanations.context: This card says what weather is.
explanations.definition: Weather is what the air and sky are like at one place and one time: sunny or cloudy, rainy or dry, windy or still, hot or cold.
explanations.description: Weather changes all the time. A morning can be sunny and the afternoon rainy. It can pour in Mumbai while Jaipur is hot and dry. We find the weather by looking at the sky, feeling the air on our skin, and watching what the wind moves.
examples: On a sunny day, shadows are dark and sharp, and the ground gets hot.
On a rainy day, puddles form and the air smells of wet earth.
On a windy day, trees sway and clothes flap on the line.
On a cloudy day, the sky is grey and shadows are soft or missing.
explanations.art: One street drawn four times: in sunshine, in rain, in wind and under clouds.

explanations.concept: Wind is moving air, and it carries warmth away
explanations.context: This card explains why a wind feels cold, after the fan test.
explanations.definition: Wind is air moving from one place to another. When moving air passes a warm body, it carries some of the body's warmth away.
explanations.description: Your body is warm. Your skin warms the thin layer of air touching it. In still air, that warm layer stays on you. Wind blows it away and brings new air. So you lose your warmth faster, and you feel cold. This works when the air is cooler than your skin. The steel tumbler is only as warm as the room. It has no extra warmth to lose.
examples: A fan feels cool on your skin, but it does not make the room colder.
On a windy beach at Kanyakumari, you can feel cool even when the air is warm.
Wet clothes feel colder in the wind than dry clothes, because the wind dries them and takes warmth from your skin.
explanations.art: A warm arm with a thin glowing layer of air around it, and arrows of wind blowing the warm air away.

explanations.concept: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water
explanations.context: This card says what clouds are, and why a cloudy day is different.
explanations.definition: A cloud is a huge crowd of tiny water drops, too small to fall, floating in the air. When the drops join into bigger, heavier drops, they fall as rain.
explanations.description: Clouds look soft, like cotton, but they are water. Each drop is much smaller than a grain of salt. A cloud spreads out the Sun's light, like a thin cloth in front of a torch. So on a cloudy day, shadows are soft and pale. Some of the Sun's light still gets through clouds. That is why you can get sunburnt on a cloudy day.
examples: Grey clouds before the monsoon are thick with water.
On a hill road in Munnar or Darjeeling, you can walk right through a cloud. It feels like cool, wet mist.
A thin white cloth held in front of a torch makes the shadow of a toy go soft, like a cloud does.
explanations.art: A white cloud in the sky with a zoom-in circle of tiny water drops, and a raindrop falling from the bottom.

explanations.concept: Clothes do a job for each kind of weather
explanations.context: This card is about choosing clothes, after the fan test.
explanations.definition: Clothes help our bodies in the weather: they keep off the sun, keep off the rain, keep out the wind, and keep in our warmth.
explanations.description: Each kind of weather needs a different job from clothes. In hot sun, a cap and loose cotton clothes shade you. In rain, a raincoat or umbrella keeps the water off. In cold, a woollen sweater keeps your warmth in. But a sweater has tiny gaps, and wind blows straight through them. So on a cold, windy day, people wear a thin layer that stops wind on top.
examples: Farmers in Kerala used the thoppikkuda, a hat made of palm leaves, shaped like a small umbrella.
Khasi farmers in Meghalaya wear the knup, a rain shield of bamboo and leaves, on their head and back. It leaves both hands free to work.
In Assam, the japi, a wide hat of bamboo and palm leaves, shades farmers from the sun.
On the cold hills of Ladakh and Sikkim, people wear a windproof jacket over their woollens.
explanations.art: Four children, each dressed for one weather: a cap and cotton for sun, a raincoat for rain, a sweater with a jacket on top for wind, and a sweater for cold.

explanations.concept: Does getting cold give you a cold?
explanations.context: This card is about something many grown-ups say: 'Wear a sweater, or you will catch a cold.'
explanations.description: A cold is an illness caused by tiny viruses, which pass from person to person. Getting chilly does not make a virus. But scientists still argue about one thing. Does being chilled make it easier for a virus you already have to make you ill?
examples: In 1968, scientists in the United States put cold viruses into people's noses, and kept some of them in the cold. The chilled people did not get more colds.
In 2005, Ron Eccles and Claire Johnson in Cardiff, Wales, had some people sit with their feet in cold water for 20 minutes. More of them got cold symptoms in the next few days.

perspectives.explanation: Colds come from viruses, not from cold weather. We catch more colds in winter and in the monsoon because people stay indoors close together, and the viruses pass more easily.
Chilling the body may make the inside of the nose colder, so it fights viruses less well. So a person who already has a virus may get ill more easily after a chill.

explanations.art: A child sneezing into their elbow on a rainy day, with tiny round viruses drawn in a zoom-in circle, and a question mark.

agreed.evidence: We cannot see air, but we see wind move leaves, clothes and kites. A fan blows air, and we feel it on our skin.

agreed.text: Wind makes a warm body lose warmth faster, but it does not make the air itself colder.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer in front of a fan reads the same as one in still air in the same room. Water in a wind freezes faster than water in still air at the same cold.

agreed.text: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water, or of tiny bits of ice high up.
agreed.evidence: Walking through a cloud on a hill feels like wet mist. Scientists in planes have flown into clouds and caught the drops.

challenging.claim: The thickest clothes keep out the wind best.
challenging.who: A very common guess, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Thick woollen clothes keep us warm on cold, still days.
challenging.against: In the fan test, wind blew straight through a thick sweater. A thin raincoat or a sheet of newspaper stopped it. What stops wind is having no gaps, not being thick.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that thick clothes stop the wind.

challenging.claim: You cannot get sunburnt on a cloudy day.
challenging.for: On a cloudy day the Sun is hidden and it often feels cooler.
challenging.against: Some of the Sun's light gets through clouds, including the part that burns skin. People do get sunburnt on cloudy days, especially on beaches and hills.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that clouds block all sunburn.

challenging.claim: Getting cold or wet gives you a cold.
challenging.who: Many families, all over the world
challenging.for: Colds are more common in cold and rainy months. A 2005 study found more cold symptoms after people chilled their feet.
challenging.against: A cold is caused by a virus that passes from person to person. A 1968 study found that chilled people who were given the virus did not get more colds.
challenging.context: This card is about a saying many grown-ups use: 'You will catch a cold.'

big_questions.q: The fan's wind cooled your arm but not the tumbler. What makes your arm different from the tumbler?
big_questions.hint: Think about which one was warm to begin with.

big_questions.q: A cloud is made of water. Why doesn't all that water fall down at once?
big_questions.hint: Think about how tiny the drops are, and what happens when they join.

big_questions.q: Your breath goes out into the air. Where does it go after that?
big_questions.hint: Think about the wind, and how air moves from place to place.

big_questions.q: Many animals have fur, feathers or thick skin for the weather. Humans have skin and hair too, and also make clothes. Why do you think we need clothes?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a crow does in the rain, and what you do.

story.title: Appa's Sweater on the Windy Hill
story.note: Meenakshi, Appa and Selvi Athai are made up. Doddabetta is a real hilltop near Ooty, and it is often cold and windy. Wind really does blow through a woollen sweater.
text: Meenakshi lived in Chennai. She was six. It was almost always warm there, so she had never worn a sweater.
At home, Meenakshi liked to hold her hands in front of the fan. 'The fan is cold,' she said. Appa smiled. 'Wait and see what wind does,' he said.
One December, the family went to Ooty, up in the hills, to visit her aunt, Selvi Athai. Selvi Athai worked in the forest and walked up and down the hills every day.
Appa packed his thickest brown sweater. 'Nothing can get through this,' he said.

The bus climbed the hill road in long curves. Halfway up, the windows went white. 'We are inside a cloud,' said Appa. Meenakshi put her hand out of the window. Tiny wet drops landed on her fingers. 'A cloud is made of water,' she said.
The next morning, Selvi Athai took them up Doddabetta, the highest hill near Ooty. The sky was blue. The wind was blowing hard.
Appa folded his arms in his thick sweater. Then he began to shiver. 'How can I be cold?' he said. 'My sweater is so thick!'
Meenakshi was cold too, in her red sweater. But Selvi Athai was not shivering. Over her old sweater she wore a thin, shiny jacket that rustled when she moved.

'Put your hand here,' said Selvi Athai. Meenakshi held her hand flat behind Appa's sweater, away from the wind. She felt cold wind coming through the wool. Then she held her hand behind Selvi Athai's jacket. No wind came through at all.
'The sweater has tiny holes between the wool!' said Meenakshi. 'The wind goes through them.'
'That is right,' said Selvi Athai. 'Wool keeps you warm on a still day. On a windy hill, the wind blows your warmth away through the holes. My jacket has no holes.'
'So it is not the thickness, Appa,' said Meenakshi. 'It is the holes.'
Selvi Athai gave Appa a spare rain jacket. He zipped it over his sweater. After a minute, he stopped shivering. 'Now my sweater can do its job,' he said, 'and the jacket can do its job.'

On the way down, they passed tea-pickers working in the wind. Each one wore a shawl, with a plastic sheet tied over it. 'Now I know why,' said Meenakshi. 'The shawl keeps the warmth in, and the plastic keeps the wind out.'

Back home in Chennai, Meenakshi held her red sweater in front of the fan and put her hand behind it. She felt the wind coming through. 'Tiny holes,' she said, and smiled. Then she held up a big plastic bag instead, and felt nothing at all. The fan was not cold. It was only moving the air.
story.epiphany: Meenakshi feels the wind coming through Appa's thick sweater but not through Athai's thin jacket. She works out that wind gets through the tiny gaps in wool, so stopping wind is about having no gaps, not about being thick.
ask: Why was Appa cold in his thick sweater?
How did Selvi Athai's thin jacket keep her warm?
What would you wear on top of your sweater on a windy hill?
art: A man in a thick brown sweater shivering on a windy hilltop, with a girl in a red sweater beside him and a woman in a thin blue jacket smiling.
A girl holding her palm flat against the back of a thick sweater on a windy hill, with little wind lines going through it.
Tea-pickers on green hills near Ooty, wearing shawls with plastic sheets tied over them.

games.title: What Will We Wear? A weather and clothes game
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A grown-up helps read the cards.
games.context: This is a card game about dressing for the weather. The 8 weather cards lie face up. The 8 clothes cards are a face-down pile. You draw a clothes card, put it beside a weather it suits, and say why.

printables.title: 8 weather cards to cut out
items: Hot sun in Chennai in May
A cold, windy hill in Ooty
A cold, still winter morning in Lucknow
A cloudy day at the beach in Puri
Rain on the hills in Meghalaya
A hot, dry, windy day in the Thar desert
A windy day by the sea in Kanyakumari

printables.title: 8 clothes cards to cut out
items: A cap and a cotton shirt
A sweater with a thin jacket on top
A cap, even though it is cloudy
A knup (a rain shield of bamboo and leaves) on your head and back
Loose cloth over your head and arms

rules: Lay the 8 weather cards face up in two rows. Mix the 8 clothes cards and make a face-down pile.
Take turns. Draw the top clothes card and read it out. The grown-up helps with reading.
Put the card beside a weather it suits, and say why. If the others agree it is a good reason, you score 1 point and the card stays there.
One weather can have more than one clothes card, if each has a good reason.

If the card suits no weather, or the others do not agree, put it face down at the bottom of the pile. The next player has a turn. If a card comes round a second time, the grown-up helps find the weather for it.
When the pile is empty, count the points. The most points wins. If points are equal, everyone wins. Then say which card was the hardest, and why.

setup.art: Eight weather cards face up in two rows on a mat, with a small pile of face-down clothes cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Weather cards face up. Clothes cards in a face-down pile.

setup.art: A child holding a raincoat card and putting it beside the card 'Heavy monsoon rain in Kochi'.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a clothes card. Put it beside a weather it suits. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Lay the 8 weather cards face up in two rows. 3. Mix the 8 clothes cards and make a face-down pile.
flow.say: Some cards show weather. Some show clothes. We need to find the weather each clothes card suits, and say why.
flow.kid: Some cards show weather. Some show clothes. Put each clothes card beside a weather it suits.

flow.do: Take turns drawing a clothes card, reading it out and putting it beside a weather it suits. Ask for a reason before the card stays.
flow.say: Do these clothes suit this weather? Why? What job do they do?
flow.kid: Draw a card. Which weather does it suit? Say why.

ask.q: Which clothes card suits more than one weather? Why?
good: The cap suits hot sun, and also a cloudy day.
A sweater suits a still cold day, and with a jacket on top it suits a windy one.

flow.parent: Good reasons: a cap and cotton shirt shade you and let sweat dry. A raincoat has no holes, so rain stays out. A sweater keeps warmth in, and a jacket on top stops the wind. A knup keeps rain off and both hands free. Loose cloth shades the skin from desert sun. A light jacket stops the wind carrying your warmth away.

flow.do: At the end, ask about the cloudy day at the beach in Puri.
flow.say: Why does the cloudy day still need a cap?
flow.kid: Why wear a cap on a cloudy day?

check.q: Why wear a cap at the beach on a cloudy day?
options: Clouds let some burning sunlight through
check.why: Some of the Sun's light that burns skin passes through clouds. A cap shades your face.

games.title: Weather Says: a moving game
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller says a weather, and everyone acts out what they would do and wear in that weather.

items.b: Put on a cap. Wipe your forehead. Walk to the shade.
Open an umbrella. Jump over a puddle.
Hold on to your cap. Lean into the wind.
Look up at the grey sky. Look for your soft shadow.
Pull on a sweater. Rub your hands together.
Pull on a sweater. Then zip a jacket over the top.

rules: Mix the 6 cards and make a pile. The caller takes the top card, reads the weather on the front aloud, and reads the back to remind everyone what to do.
Everyone else acts it out, with pretend things. No real umbrella or sweater is needed.
The caller can call two cards fast, one after the other. Put used cards at the bottom of the pile.
Each caller calls 3 cards, then the next player becomes the caller. The game ends when everyone has been the caller once.

setup.art: A small group of children in a living room, one holding up a card that says 'Windy!'.
setup.caption: 1. The caller calls a weather.

setup.art: Children leaning forward and holding on to pretend caps, as if in a strong wind.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone acts it out.

flow.do: Cut out the six cards. Read the backs aloud so everyone knows the actions.
flow.say: When I call a weather, show me what you would wear and do.
flow.kid: Listen to the weather. Show what you would wear and do.

flow.do: Call the cards one at a time, then faster. Let each player be the caller for 3 cards.
flow.say: Windy! Now cold and windy! What do you put on top?
flow.kid: Act out each weather. Be quick!

experiments.title: The Fan and the Sweater: which clothes stop the wind?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a wind with a fan. First you find out if the wind cools a steel tumbler, or only you. Then you hold up different clothes in the wind, and use a paper strip to see which ones let the wind through. Last, you feel what wind does to a wet hand.
experiments.question: Does the fan's wind make things colder, or only warm bodies like you? Which clothes stop the wind: a thin dupatta, a thick sweater, a raincoat or a newspaper? Does wind feel colder on a wet hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the tumbler in the wind get cold? Which cloth will stop the wind best? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The fan stays on the same speed. Each cloth is held at the same place, one arm's length from the fan. The paper strip is held just behind the middle of each cloth, a finger's width away. Only the cloth changes.
results_table: Did the paper strip move? A lot, a little, or still
How did my arm feel behind it?

materials.item: a table fan or a pedestal fan (or a ceiling fan, see the note in step 2)
a strip of tissue or thin paper, 2 fingers wide and as long as your hand, taped to a pencil
a thin cotton dupatta or a thin cotton T-shirt
a woollen sweater or a woollen shawl
a raincoat, or a big plastic carry bag cut open into a flat sheet
a bowl of water and a towel

experiments.safety: Keep fingers, hair, the dupatta and the paper strip away from the fan blades. Keep the bowl of water well away from the fan and any socket. Never put a plastic bag over anyone's head or face.

schedule.what: Leave a tumbler in the fan's wind for 5 minutes. Feel it. Test each cloth with the paper strip, and feel it on your arm. Last, compare a wet hand and a dry hand in the wind.

experiments.record: Draw the fan, the cloth and the paper strip for each test. Draw the strip flying for 'a lot', and hanging down for 'still'.

setup.art: A table fan blowing on a steel tumbler on a stool, with a second tumbler standing on a shelf far from the fan.
setup.caption: 1. Put one tumbler in the fan's wind and one far away. Wait 5 minutes.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a woollen sweater flat in front of a table fan, and a child holding a paper strip on a pencil just behind it. The strip is fluttering.
setup.caption: 2. Hold up a cloth. Hold the paper strip just behind it.

setup.art: The same scene with a raincoat held up instead. The paper strip hangs straight down.
setup.caption: 3. Try each cloth. Does the strip move or hang still?

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan on to medium. 2. Put one steel tumbler on a stool, an arm's length in front of the fan. 3. Put the other tumbler far away, in another room or a far corner.
flow.say: One tumbler sits in the fan's wind. The other sits far away. We will leave them for five minutes.
flow.kid: Put one tumbler in front of the fan. Put the other one far away.
flow.parent: Use dry tumblers that have been in the house for a while, so both start as warm as the room.

flow.do: 1. While you wait for the 5 minutes, ask your child to hold a bare arm in the fan's wind. 2. Ask what they think will happen to the tumbler, and why. 3. Show the paper strip: it flies in the wind. Ask which cloth will stop the wind, and why.
flow.say: How does your arm feel in the wind? Will the tumbler in the wind get cold too? Why? This paper strip is our wind finder. It flies in wind and hangs down in still air. Which cloth will stop the wind best? Why?
flow.kid: Hold your arm in the wind. Will the tumbler get cold too? Which cloth will stop the wind? Why?

ask.q: Will the tumbler in the wind get cold? Why?
good: Yes, because the wind is cold.
No, because the fan doesn't make cold.

ask.q: Which cloth will stop the wind best? Why?
good: The sweater, because it is thickest.
The raincoat, because water can't get through it.

flow.parent: Most children guess the tumbler will get cold, and that the thick sweater will stop the wind. Write the guesses down. Don't say what will happen. With only a ceiling fan, stand under it. Hold each cloth flat like a roof, and hang the strip just under its middle.

flow.do: After five minutes, ask your child to touch the tumbler in the wind, then the tumbler far away. Then hold a hand in the wind again.
flow.say: Touch the tumbler from the fan. Now touch the one from far away. Is one colder? Now put your hand in the wind. How does it feel?
flow.kid: Touch both tumblers. Is one colder? Now feel the wind on your hand.

ask.q: Did the wind make the tumbler colder?
good: No, they feel the same.
No, but my hand feels cold in the wind.

check.q: The tumbler sat in the fan's wind for five minutes. How did it feel?
options: Much colder than the other tumbler
The same as the other tumbler
check.why: The fan moves the room's air, but it does not make it colder. The tumbler was as warm as the room, so it had no extra warmth to lose. Your warm hand did, so it felt cold.

flow.parent: Both tumblers feel the same, a little cool, as steel always does. That is the surprise. The fan cools your hand because your hand is warmer than the air.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up holds each cloth flat, one arm's length in front of the fan. 2. Your child holds the strip just behind the middle of the cloth. 3. Try nothing, the dupatta, the sweater, the raincoat and the newspaper, in turn.
flow.say: Hold the strip just behind the cloth. Watch it. Does it fly, wave a little, or hang still?
flow.kid: Hold the strip just behind the cloth. Does it fly? Or hang still?

ask.q: What did the strip do behind the sweater?
good: It still moved.
It waved, so wind came through.

ask.q: What did it do behind the raincoat?
good: It hung still.
No wind came through.

flow.parent: Hold the cloth bigger than the strip, so wind does not curl round the edge. If the strip twitches a little behind the raincoat, that is air curling round the edges. Compare it with the sweater.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts on the sweater and holds that arm in the wind. 2. Then the grown-up wraps the raincoat or plastic sheet over the sweater sleeve. 3. Hold the arm in the wind again.
flow.say: Feel the wind through the sweater. Now we put the raincoat over the top. What changed? Why did wind go through the sweater but not the raincoat?
flow.kid: Feel the wind through your sweater. Now cover it with the raincoat. What changed? Why?

ask.q: Why did your arm feel warmer with the raincoat on top?
good: The raincoat stopped the wind.
The wind couldn't take my warmth away.

ask.q: Why did wind go through the sweater but not the raincoat?
good: The sweater has tiny holes between the wool.
The raincoat has no holes.

flow.parent: Wrap the plastic round the arm only. Two layers, wool inside and a wind-stopper outside, is how people dress on cold, windy hills.
flow.think: The wind cooled your arm but not the tumbler. What was different about your arm?

flow.do: 1. Dip the fingers of one hand in the bowl of water. Keep the other hand dry. 2. Hold both hands out in the fan's wind for half a minute. 3. Feel which hand is colder. 4. Then move away from the fan, into still air, and feel again. 5. Dry your hands on the towel.
flow.say: One hand is wet and one is dry. Hold them both in the wind. Which one feels colder? Now move away from the fan. Is it still colder?
flow.kid: Wet one hand. Hold both hands in the wind. Which one feels colder?

ask.q: Which hand felt colder in the wind? Why?
good: The wet hand. The wind dried the water and took my warmth.
The wet hand, because drying takes warmth from my skin.

flow.parent: The wet hand feels colder in still air too, but much colder in the wind. Wet clothes feel cold in the wind for the same reason.

activities.title: Weather Detectives: find clues indoors
activities.context: In this activity you hunt round your home for clues about today's weather, before you look at the sky. Then you check at the window.

schedule.what: Hunt for weather clues indoors. Then look out of the window to check.

activities.record: Draw the best clue you found, and the weather you think it shows.

setup.art: A child looking at wet chappals and a dripping umbrella by a front door.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt for clues indoors: umbrellas, chappals, curtains, light on the floor.

setup.art: The same child at a window, pointing at grey clouds and a wet road.
setup.caption: 2. Look out of the window. Were you right?

flow.do: Walk round the home together, without looking out of a window. Look for clues: a wet umbrella, damp chappals, a curtain moving, a bright patch of sun on the floor, clothes drying.
flow.say: Let's be weather detectives. Without looking at the sky, what clues tell us about the weather today?
flow.kid: Find weather clues inside your home. Do not look at the sky yet.

ask.q: What does this clue tell us?
good: A wet umbrella means it rained.
The curtain is moving, so it is windy.
A bright patch on the floor means it is sunny.

flow.do: Go to a window. Look at the sky, the trees and the road. Ask your child if the clues were right.
flow.say: Now look outside. Is it sunny, rainy, windy or cloudy? Did our clues tell the truth?
flow.kid: Look outside. Is it sunny, rainy, windy or cloudy? Were your clues right?
flow.parent: Sometimes it is two at once, like sunny and windy. That is fine. Let your child say both.

activities.title: A Cloud for the Torch: why are shadows soft on a cloudy day?
activities.context: In this activity you shine a torch on a toy to make a sharp shadow, like on a sunny day. Then you hold a thin white cloth in front of the torch, like a cloud, and watch the shadow change.

materials.item: a torch, or the torch on a phone
a thin white cloth, a white hanky, or butter paper
a white wall or a sheet of white paper

schedule.what: Make a sharp shadow with the torch. Then put a 'cloud' in front of the torch and look again.

activities.record: Draw the sharp shadow and the soft shadow side by side.

setup.art: A torch shining on a small toy elephant in a dim room, making a sharp dark shadow on a white wall.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch on a toy. Look at the sharp shadow.

setup.art: The same toy with a white hanky held in front of the torch, and a soft pale shadow on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the thin cloth a hand's width in front of the torch. Look again.

flow.do: 1. Dim the room. 2. Stand the toy a hand-length in front of the white wall. 3. Shine the torch on the toy from about one arm's length away.
flow.say: The torch is our Sun. Look at the toy's shadow. Is the edge sharp or fuzzy?
flow.kid: The torch is the Sun. Look at the shadow. Is the edge sharp?

flow.do: Hold the thin white cloth flat, a hand's width in front of the torch, so the light passes through it. Ask your child to guess first what will happen to the shadow.
flow.say: This cloth is our cloud. What do you think will happen to the shadow? Why? Now let's look.
flow.kid: The cloth is a cloud. What will happen to the shadow? Look!

good: It went pale and fuzzy.
It almost went away.

flow.parent: The cloth makes the light come from a wide patch, not one bright spot, so the edge of the shadow goes soft. If the edge does not change, move the toy a little further from the wall. A real cloud does the same to sunlight.

flow.do: Next time it is cloudy, look at your own shadow outside or on the balcony floor.
flow.say: On a cloudy day, look for your shadow. Will it be sharp or soft?
flow.kid: On a cloudy day, look for your shadow. Sharp or soft?
flow.wait: Do this on the next cloudy day. If it is cloudy now, do it now.

activities.title: Sort the Cupboard: clothes for each weather
activities.context: In this activity you take clothes out of the family cupboard and sort them into piles: for sun, for rain, for wind and for cold. You say what job each one does.

materials.item: clothes from the cupboard: caps, cotton clothes, sweaters, shawls, a raincoat, an umbrella, chappals, socks
4 sheets of paper with a sun, a raincloud, wind lines and a snowflake drawn on them

schedule.what: Sort clothes into four weather piles and say the job of each one.

activities.record: Draw one thing from each pile.

setup.art: Four papers on the floor with a sun, a raincloud, wind lines and a snowflake, and a pile of mixed clothes beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Put down the four weather papers. Bring out the clothes.

setup.art: A child putting a cap on the sun paper and an umbrella on the raincloud paper.
setup.caption: 2. Put each thing on a weather paper. Say its job.

flow.do: Lay out the four papers. Your child picks one thing at a time, puts it on a paper, and says its job.
flow.say: Which weather is this for? What job does it do? Does it keep off the sun, the rain or the wind, or keep warmth in?
flow.kid: Pick a thing. Which weather is it for? What job does it do?

ask.q: What job does a cap do?
good: It shades my head from the sun.
It keeps the sun out of my eyes.

flow.parent: Some things fit two piles. A raincoat works in rain and in wind. Let your child put it between the two papers and say why.

flow.do: Hold up the sweater. Ask which pile it goes on, and what it can't do. Remind your child of the fan test if you have done it.
flow.say: The sweater keeps us warm. But what happened when the fan blew on it? What could we wear on top on a windy day?
flow.kid: Where does the sweater go? What can you wear on top when it is windy?

ask.q: What can we wear over a sweater on a windy day?
good: A raincoat.
A jacket with no holes.

projects.title: Dress the Window Doll: five mornings
projects.context: In this project you make a paper doll and paper clothes. Each morning for five days, you look out of the window and dress the doll for the weather. On the last day you count the kinds of weather.

materials.item: card or a cereal box, for the doll
a little tape or a hair clip to hold the clothes on

schedule.what: Make the doll and clothes: a cap, a cotton dress or shirt, a raincoat, a sweater and a jacket. Dress the doll for today.
Look out. Dress the doll. Draw today's weather picture on the chart.
Look out. Dress the doll. Draw today's weather picture.
Look out. Dress the doll. Draw today's weather picture.
Dress the doll. Count each kind of weather on the chart.

projects.record: A chart with five boxes, one for each morning, with a weather picture in each.

setup.art: A paper doll made from card with paper clothes beside her: a cap, a cotton dress, a raincoat, a sweater and a jacket.
setup.caption: 1. Make a paper doll and clothes for every weather.

setup.art: The paper doll taped by a window wearing a raincoat, and a chart with five boxes below, three with suns and two with rain clouds.
setup.caption: 2. Each morning, look out, dress the doll and draw the weather.

flow.do: 1. Draw and cut out a doll from card. 2. Draw and cut out a cap, a cotton dress or shirt, a raincoat, a sweater and a jacket. 3. Give the doll a name. 4. Draw a chart with five boxes. 5. Dress the doll for today and draw today's weather in box 1.
flow.say: This doll will live by our window. Every morning we will dress her for the weather. What clothes will she need?
flow.kid: Make a doll. Make clothes for sun, rain, wind and cold.

ask.q: What clothes will the doll need?
good: A cap for sun.
A raincoat for rain.
A jacket for wind.

flow.parent: You may draw the chart and the boxes. Let your child draw the weather pictures and choose the clothes.

flow.wait: Come back each morning on days 2, 3 and 4.
flow.do: Each morning, look out of the window together. Your child says the weather, dresses the doll and draws a weather picture in that day's box.
flow.say: What is the weather this morning? What will the doll wear? Why?
flow.kid: Look out. What is the weather? Dress the doll. Draw the weather.
flow.parent: If the weather is mixed, let your child draw both, like a sun behind a cloud.

flow.do: Dress the doll and draw today's weather in the last box. Then count the sunny, rainy, windy and cloudy boxes on the chart.
flow.say: Let's count. How many sunny mornings? How many rainy ones? Which weather came most?
flow.kid: Count the suns. Count the clouds. Which came most?

ask.q: Did the weather stay the same all week?
good: No, it changed.
It was sunny most days.

challenges.title: A Rain Hat That Stays On in the Wind
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Make a rain hat for a toy that keeps the water off, and does not blow away in the fan's wind.
challenges.problem: Your toy needs a hat for a rainy, windy day, like the knup that Khasi farmers wear in Meghalaya. The hat must keep water off the toy's head, and stay on in front of the fan.
constraints: The hat must stay on for 10 seconds in front of the fan.
A spoon of water poured on top, away from the fan, must not reach the toy's head.
materials: a small plastic toy that can get wet
paper, a paper plate, a leaf or a piece of plastic bag
tape, string or a rubber band
a spoon and a cup of water
a tray or a big bowl
general: Make a cone from a paper plate, so the water runs off the edge.
Tie the hat on with string under the toy's chin.
Make the hat wide, so the water drips off away from the toy.
creative: Make the hat low and curved, so the wind slides over it instead of lifting it.
Cover a paper hat with a piece of plastic bag, so it does not go soggy.
Make a hat that covers the head and the back, like a knup.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own rain hat. Draw it, make it and test it with the fan and the spoon of water. What would you change?

setup.art: A small toy wearing a cone-shaped paper plate hat tied with string, standing in front of a table fan.
setup.caption: 1. Make a hat and tie it on. Test it in the fan's wind.

setup.art: A child pouring a spoon of water onto the toy's hat, with the drops running off the edge.
setup.caption: 2. Away from the fan, pour a spoon of water on top. Is the toy's head dry?

flow.do: Show your child the problem. A knup is a rain shield of bamboo and leaves that Khasi farmers wear on the head and back. Talk about why it suits rain and wind.
flow.say: This toy needs a hat for a rainy, windy day. It must keep the water off and stay on in the wind. How could we make one?
flow.kid: Make a rain hat for your toy. It must stay on in the wind.

flow.do: Your child chooses an idea, or invents one, and makes the hat.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? What shape will let the water run off?
flow.kid: Choose an idea. Make your hat.
flow.parent: Help with tying or tape if needed, but let your child choose the shape.

flow.do: 1. Put the toy in front of the fan for 10 seconds. 2. Carry it far from the fan, over the tray. 3. Pour one spoon of water on top of the hat. 4. Feel the toy's head.
flow.say: Did the hat stay on? Is the toy's head dry? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did the hat stay on? Is the head dry? What will you change?

ask.q: What shape works best in the wind?
good: A low, curved hat.
A hat tied on with string.

challenges.safety: Pour the water far away from the fan and any socket, over the tray.

items.p: Draw a line from each weather to its picture.
pairs: A bright sun and a dark, sharp shadow
A tree bending and clothes flapping
A grey sky and a soft shadow
items.why: Each weather has its own clues. A sharp shadow means sun. A bending tree means wind.
items.art: Four pictures: a sun with a sharp shadow, rain with a puddle, a bending tree, a grey sky.

items.p: Remember the fan test? One tumbler stood in the fan's wind for five minutes. How did it feel next to the other tumbler?
items.why: The fan moves air but does not make it colder. The tumbler was as warm as the room, so it had no extra warmth to lose.

items.p: Draw the paper strip behind the sweater, and behind the raincoat. Show what each strip did.
items.a: Behind the sweater, the strip waves or flies. Behind the raincoat, the strip hangs straight down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference: wind came through the sweater's tiny gaps, but not through the raincoat.
items.art: Two empty boxes, one with a sweater drawn at the top and one with a raincoat.

items.p: Circle the things that let wind through. Put a box round the things that stop it.
items.why: Cloth made of threads has tiny gaps, so wind gets through. Plastic and paper sheets have no gaps.
items.art: Six small pictures: a sweater, a raincoat, a dupatta, a newspaper, a T-shirt and a plastic sheet.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why did your arm feel cold in the fan's wind?
items.a: The wind carried warmth away from my warm arm.
items.why: A strong answer says the wind took warmth away from the arm, not that the wind was cold.

items.p: Tea-pickers tie plastic sheets over their shawls in the rain. A plastic sheet keeps the rain out because it has no holes.
items.why: True. Rain and wind cannot get through a sheet with no holes. A cloth shawl has tiny gaps, so it soaks up water and lets wind through.

items.p: Here is a child on a cold, windy hill. Colour red the layer that keeps warmth in. Colour blue the layer that stops the wind.
items.a: The sweater is red and the thin jacket on top is blue.
items.why: The sweater holds warmth in. The jacket on top stops the wind blowing that warmth away.
items.art: A child on a hill wearing a sweater with a thin jacket over it, both drawn as plain outlines to colour in.

items.p: Which one is NOT for a rainy day?
items.why: A woollen shawl soaks up water. A raincoat, an umbrella and a knup all keep the rain off.

items.p: Draw yourself dressed for a hot, sunny day in May.
items.a: A drawing with a cap or hat and light, loose clothes, maybe in the shade.
items.why: A strong drawing shows something to shade the head, and light clothes that let sweat dry.

items.p: Two friends in Bengaluru are going up a cold, windy hill.

views.says: I will wear my thickest sweater. Nothing else.
I will wear a thin sweater and a raincoat on top.

items.ask: Who will be warmer in the wind? Use what you saw in the fan test. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Farhan will be warmer in the wind, because the raincoat stops the wind. But Divya is right that a thick sweater keeps warmth in well on a still day.
items.why: A strong answer uses the fan test: wind went through the sweater but not the raincoat. It is also fair to Divya: wool is good at keeping warmth in.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Kolkata, stands in front of the fan with wet hands. Her friend stands there with dry hands. Who feels colder?
items.why: The wind dries the water on Nandini's hands, and drying takes warmth from her skin. That is also why wet clothes feel cold in the wind.

items.p: In the fan test, why did we hold every cloth at the same place, one arm's length from the fan? Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down.
items.a: So that only the cloth is different. If one cloth were closer to the fan, it could look different only because of where it was.
items.why: A strong answer says that only one thing should change in a fair test.

items.p: Put the pictures in order, from first to last.
items: A cloud of tiny drops floats in the sky
The tiny drops join and grow bigger
a: A cloud of tiny drops floats in the sky
The tiny drops join and grow bigger
items.why: Cloud drops are too small to fall. When they join into bigger, heavier drops, they fall as rain.
items.art: Three pictures: rain falling, a white cloud, a cloud with bigger drops inside.

items.p: Remember the torch and the white cloth? What did the cloth do to the toy's shadow?
items.why: The cloth spread out the torch's light, like a cloud spreads sunlight. So the shadow went soft.

items.p: You can get sunburnt on a cloudy day.
items.why: True. Some of the Sun's light that burns skin gets through clouds.

items.p: Draw a cloud. Then draw a zoom-in circle next to it, showing what a cloud is made of.
items.a: A cloud with a circle full of tiny round water drops.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a cloud is made of many tiny drops of water.
items.art: An empty sky with space for a cloud and a circle.

items.p: Draw a line from each rain shield to where people wear it.
items.why: People all over India made clever hats and shields from plants that grow near them.
items.art: Three hats: a curved shield on a person's back, a small palm-leaf umbrella hat and a wide round bamboo hat.

items.p: Here is the fan test. Colour the fan yellow, the paper strip green and the cloth purple.
items.a: The fan is yellow, the paper strip behind the cloth is green and the cloth held in front is purple.
items.why: The fan makes the wind, the cloth is tested, and the strip shows if wind came through.
items.art: A fan, a cloth held in front of it and a paper strip on a pencil behind it, drawn as plain outlines to colour in.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, says: 'My sweater is so thick, no wind can get through it.' What would you tell Kavya? Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down.
items.a: In the fan test, wind came through the thick sweater. It has tiny gaps between the wool. A thin raincoat on top would stop the wind.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence from the test, not only an opinion, and suggests what would work.

items.p: Which one tells you it is windy?
items.why: You cannot see wind, but you can see what it moves. A sharp shadow means sun, a puddle means rain and a grey sky means clouds.

videos.title: What is wind? A short film for young children
videos.why: Shows that wind is moving air, with things it moves: leaves, kites, clothes.
videos.check: Find a real, accurate video for age 6. Check it does not say that wind is 'cold air' only.

videos.title: Walking through a cloud on a hill
videos.why: Shows that a cloud is wet mist made of water drops.
videos.check: Find real footage of fog or a cloud on a hill road, for example in Munnar, Ooty or Meghalaya.

videos.title: How the knup rain shield is made in Meghalaya
videos.why: Shows a real rain shield made of bamboo and leaves, worn so both hands stay free.
videos.check: Find a real video of knup making. Check it is from Meghalaya and shows the real materials.

quiz.why: Wind is air that is moving. We can't see air, but we see what wind moves.

quiz.p: Which is a kind of weather?
quiz.why: Rainy is a kind of weather. Sleepy and hungry are how a body feels.

quiz.p: In the fan test, what did the paper strip do behind the raincoat?
quiz.why: The raincoat has no gaps, so the wind could not get through. The strip hung still.

quiz.p: Which lets the most wind through?
quiz.why: Wool has tiny gaps between the threads, and wind blows through them. Newspaper and plastic have no gaps.

quiz.p: Why does the fan make your arm feel cold?
opts: The moving air carries your warmth away
The fan is made of ice
quiz.why: Your arm is warmer than the air. The moving air keeps carrying that warmth away.

quiz.p: What is a cloud made of?
quiz.why: A cloud is millions of tiny water drops floating in the air. It only looks like cotton.

quiz.p: Lakshmi is going out in the hot May sun in Madurai. What should she wear?
opts: A cap and loose cotton clothes
quiz.why: A cap shades her head, and loose cotton lets her sweat dry and cool her.

quiz.p: It is cold and windy on a hill. What should Anjali wear?
opts: A sweater with a jacket on top
quiz.why: The sweater keeps her warmth in. The jacket on top stops the wind blowing it away.

quiz.p: What are shadows like on a cloudy day?
quiz.why: Clouds spread out the Sun's light, so shadows go soft and pale.

quiz.p: Rani guessed the sweater would stop the wind. In the test, wind came through it. What should Rani do?
opts: Change her idea to fit what she saw
quiz.why: A good scientist changes her idea when the test shows something new. A wrong guess helps you learn.

applications: People on cold, windy hills wear a windproof jacket over their woollens.
Weather reports on TV and phones tell families what to wear for the day.
Farmers use the weather to choose when to sow seeds, and when to keep a harvest dry.
Anna Mani, an Indian scientist, designed weather instruments at the India Meteorological Department. She also set up wind measuring across India, to find good places for windmills.

spotted.text: Clothes flapping on a balcony line on a windy afternoon.
spotted.art: Colourful clothes flapping on a line across a flat's balcony, with a tree swaying behind.

spotted.text: Shopkeepers hanging plastic sheets over their stalls when the monsoon comes.
spotted.art: A street stall with a blue plastic sheet tied over it in the rain.

spotted.text: Tea-pickers on the hills of Munnar or Darjeeling with plastic sheets over their heads and backs in the rain.
spotted.art: Tea-pickers on a green slope in the rain, with plastic sheets over their heads and baskets.

spotted.text: Grandparents wearing a monkey cap and a shawl on a cold winter morning walk.
spotted.art: An old woman in a shawl and a woollen monkey cap walking in the early morning mist.

spotted.text: A soft, pale shadow under a tree on a cloudy day.
spotted.art: A tree on a grey day with a very faint, soft shadow underneath.

open_questions.q: Does getting chilled make it easier for a cold virus to make you ill?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies found more cold symptoms after people were chilled, and others found no difference. Scientists still argue about it.

open_questions.q: Exactly when and where will it rain tomorrow?
open_questions.why_open: Weather forecasts get better every year, but rain is still hard to predict exactly, place by place.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be the wind, or a cloud?
open_questions.why_open: Everything is conscious in its own way, but nobody knows what that is like for moving air or water drops.

ask_kids: What is the weather doing right now? How can you tell?
What would you wear if it rained right now?
Where does the wind go after it blows past our window?
Why does a fan feel cool on a hot day?
Is your shadow sharp or soft today?

jokes.j: What did one cloud say to the other cloud?
jokes.a: Let's stick together and make rain!

jokes.j: Why did the sweater go to the windy hill?
jokes.a: To get some fresh air, right through its holes!

jokes.j: What does the wind wear on a cold day?
jokes.a: Nothing. It just blows straight through everyone else's sweaters!

jokes.j: Why did the umbrella stay at home?
jokes.a: It was too sunny to go out.

jokes.j: What did the fan say to the boy?
jokes.a: I'm not cold. You're just warm!

jokes.j: How do clouds go to the bathroom?
What did the Sun say to the cloud?
jokes.a: Move over, I want to see the children!

jokes.j: What is a cloud's favourite game?
jokes.a: Hide and seek with the Sun!

maths.problem: Meera dressed her window doll for five mornings. 3 mornings were sunny and 2 were rainy. Were there more sunny mornings or rainy mornings? How many more?
maths.answer: More sunny mornings. There was 1 more sunny morning than rainy mornings.
maths.explain: 3 sunny and 2 rainy. 3 is more than 2. 3 take away 2 is 1.
maths.context: This is about the window doll chart from the five-morning project.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the counts shows which weather came most that week.

maths.problem: In the fan test, Priya tested 5 things. The paper strip moved behind 3 of them. Behind how many did it hang still?
maths.answer: 2 things. The strip hung still behind 2 things, the raincoat and the newspaper.
maths.explain: 5 things take away the 3 where the strip moved leaves 2.
maths.context: This is about the fan test, where a paper strip showed if wind came through each cloth.
maths.why_maths: Counting the results tells us how many things stopped the wind.

maths.problem: Sort these 8 weather pictures and make a tally: sun, sun, rain, cloud, sun, rain, sun, cloud. How many of each?
maths.answer: Sun: 4. Rain: 2. Cloud: 2. That makes 8 in all.
maths.explain: Make one tally mark for each picture under its kind. Count the marks. 4 + 2 + 2 = 8, which checks we counted every picture.
maths.context: This is like the weather chart from the window doll project.
maths.why_maths: A tally lets us count many weather days quickly and see which weather is most common.

maths.problem: In Kochi in July, it rains on most days. Is it likely or unlikely that it will rain tomorrow in Kochi?
maths.answer: Likely. Rain comes on most July days in Kochi, but not on every one.
maths.explain: Something that happens on most days is likely, but not certain. So it will probably rain, and it might not.
maths.context: This is about the monsoon in Kerala, where it rains a lot in June and July.
maths.why_maths: Weather is never certain, so we use words like likely and might to say how sure we are.

warmup.q: What is a cloud made of?
Does a fan make the air colder?
warmup.a: No. It moves the air, and the moving air takes warmth from your skin.

warmup.q: What stops the wind better: a sweater or a raincoat?
warmup.a: A raincoat. Wind goes through the gaps in a sweater.

warmup.q: Can you get sunburnt on a cloudy day?
warmup.a: Yes. Some sunlight gets through clouds.

founder: No by_topic file exists for weather. Used ideas/by_topic/caring-for-the-environment.md ('Keep a notebook of daily weather'), turned into the window doll project for Class 1.
ideas/by_topic/body-parts-and-skeleton.md art idea 'Draw you in three weathers', used as worksheet drawing items.

Ladder: Level 3 (sci.weather.weather.L3) measures weather with a thermometer, rain gauge and wind vane, with a sun-or-shade thermometer test. This unit does no measuring and repeats none of its experiments. It leads on to it by noticing the four weathers and what wind does.
science: Wind chill: moving air increases heat loss from a body warmer than the air (forced convection). It does not lower the air temperature, and a dry object at room temperature is not cooled below it. A fan adds a little heat to a room.

Paul Siple and Charles Passel, 'Measurements of dry atmospheric cooling in subfreezing temperatures', Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 89 (1945). Water (about 250 g) in a plastic cylinder, timed to freeze in about 100 combinations of wind and temperature, at Little America III during the US Antarctic Service Expedition (1939 to 1941).
The 2001 Wind Chill Temperature index (Canada and the United States) was based on tests with volunteers' faces in a cold wind tunnel.
Knitted wool is highly air-permeable. Wind-resistant shells (tightly woven or coated fabrics) are worn over insulating layers.

Clouds are made of water droplets (typically about 0.01 to 0.02 mm across) or ice crystals. Diffuse light under cloud gives soft shadows. Much ultraviolet light passes through thin or broken cloud, so sunburn is possible on cloudy days.

R. G. Douglas and others, 'Exposure to cold environment and rhinovirus common cold: failure to demonstrate effect', New England Journal of Medicine 279 (1968). C. Johnson and R. Eccles, 'Acute cooling of the feet and the onset of common cold symptoms', Family Practice 22 (2005), Cardiff University.
Knup: Khasi rain shield of bamboo and leaves (Ministry of Culture, India, Exhibit of the week 167, 2023). Japi: Assamese hat of bamboo and palm leaves. Thoppikkuda: Kerala palm-leaf hat-umbrella.
Anna Mani (1918 to 2001), physicist and meteorologist at the India Meteorological Department, worked on Indian-made weather instruments and on wind energy and solar radiation measurements.

Chandogya Upanishad 4.3.1 (the samvarga teaching of Raikva: the wind takes in fire, Sun and Moon). Tao Te Ching 23 (a whirlwind does not last a whole morning, a sudden rain does not last a whole day).
Doddabetta, the highest peak of the Nilgiris, about 2,637 m.

roots.context: We have felt the fan's wind cool our arm, but not the steel tumbler. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the fan's wind your bare arm felt cold, yet the steel tumbler beside it got no colder. The moving air was the same air as the rest of the room. It carried warmth away from your warm arm, and the tumbler had no extra warmth to lose. So wind chills only what is warmer than the air, like you.
deep_truth.habit: We say a windy day is 'cold', as if the wind brings coldness with it. Most of the time the wind is the same air, only moving. What changes is how fast it carries warmth away from our warm bodies.
deep_truth.evidence: In the fan test, a steel tumbler stood in the fan's wind for five minutes. It felt just like a tumbler kept far from the fan. A bare arm in the same wind felt cold within a minute.

three.who_am_i: You are warm all the time, warmer than the air around you. Your body makes that warmth from your food.
three.what_is_life: A living body keeps making warmth and giving it away. The wind takes it, and food makes more.
three.what_is_this_world: The same air wraps the whole Earth, and it is always moving. Today's wind in your city will be somewhere else tomorrow.

roots.thread: One layer of air wraps the whole Earth. The same air is a still afternoon in Chennai, a sea breeze in Kochi and a cold wind on a pass in Ladakh. Your warmth goes out into that air, and the wind carries it on. Your breath joins it too. Everything in the world is conscious, the moving air too, in its own way.

teachings.teaching: The wind is the one that takes everything in. When a fire goes out, it goes into the wind. When the Sun sets and the Moon sets, they go into the wind.
teachings.link: In the fan test, the wind took the warmth from your arm into the room's air. A fire's heat goes into the air in the same way.

teachings.teaching: A strong wind does not last the whole morning. A sudden rain does not last the whole day.
teachings.link: Weather is always changing. That is why we look outside each morning before we choose our clothes.

science.text: Wind cools a warm body faster, but it does not lower the temperature of the air. A fan makes a room no colder.
What moving air is like from the inside, and how the air senses the world, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Most scientists say wind is only air moving from one place to another, pushed by warm and cool places. They say air has no awareness of any kind, and that only living bodies with nerves feel things.

practice.title: Feel your own warmth
practice.say: Hold your hand a finger's width from your cheek. Do not touch. Can you feel warmth? That is your own warmth. Now wave a piece of paper like a fan between your hand and your cheek. What happens? The moving air carried your warmth away.
practice.kid: Hold your hand near your cheek. Do not touch. Feel the warmth? Now wave a paper between them. What changes?

ask: Where does the warmth go, after the wind carries it away from you?
Is the wind one thing, or a lot of air passing by?
If you could ask the wind one question, what would you ask?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out how much the wind cools us? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: People in cold places knew that a windy day feels far colder than a still day, even when a thermometer reads the same. Around 1940, two men tested this in Antarctica. Paul Siple was an American explorer. Charles Passel was a scientist on the same expedition. At their camp, Little America III, they filled a plastic tube with about 250 grams of water and hung it outside. They timed how long it took to freeze. They did this about a hundred times, in still air and in strong wind. In strong wind, the water froze much faster, though the thermometer read the same. In 1945 they published their results. These became the 'wind chill' numbers in weather reports. Later, scientists found that a tube of water loses warmth faster than skin does. So in 2001, new numbers were worked out from tests on real people's faces.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Siple, an American explorer, and Charles Passel, a scientist on the same expedition to Antarctica
how_we_found_out.when: Their tests were around 1940, at Little America III in Antarctica. They published them in 1945. New wind chill numbers came in 2001.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a thermometer alone tells how cold it is for a body. At the same thermometer reading, water froze much faster in the wind, so wind matters too.
how_we_found_out.art: Two explorers in thick fur-lined coats on the snow, looking up at a small tube of water hanging from a tall pole in the wind.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and a 6-year-old would, with a fan, steel tumblers, cloth and a paper strip in a flat. Rebuilt the clothes game so it has a face-down pile, an ending and a winner with 2 or 4 players, and gave the moving game a clear end. Made the fan test 22 minutes with a 5-minute wait that really fits, and added the wet-hand test. Fixed the water-near-the-fan step in the hat challenge, lengthened the story, and removed repeated questions, weak jokes and unintroduced names.
